title: Princeton alumni deploy ultrahydrophobic filters to capture microplastics in Atlantic City wastewater
body:
Former Princeton University graduates have deployed a new filtration technology at the Atlantic County Utilities Authority's wastewater treatment plant to remove microplastics [1]. The system, developed by PolyGone Systems, was designed to prevent these contaminants from entering the Atlantic Ocean [1]. Plastics do not biodegrade but break down into smaller fragments known as microplastics that persist in the environment and accumulate in living organisms [1].

## How the technology works

The technology replicates ultrahydrophobic plants found in wetlands, allowing microplastics to stick to it for removal [4]. This mechanism mimics natural processes where specific plant structures attract and capture contaminants [9]. The filter is made of thousands of silicone fibers that trap small particles due to their hydrophobic properties [14]. Microplastics adhere to the bristly brush-like structure while wastewater flows through [14].

## Development and funding

PolyGone Systems is a startup founded by Nathanial Banks and Yidian Liu, who are former Princeton graduates [4]. The company was established in 2021 and is based in Kearny, New Jersey [7]. Both founders are Forbes 30 under 30 fellows [11]. The startup raised $4 million in seed funding to expand its filtration capabilities [7]. This round included participation from Tech Council Ventures, FYRFLY Venture Partners, and Golden Seeds [8].

## Implementation at Atlantic City

The installation at the Atlantic County Utilities Authority facility is believed to be the world's first permanent operation of its kind [12]. The project follows a two-year pilot program that began in 2024 [12]. Over the course of the next year, their filter pulled more than half a billion pieces of tiny plastic from ocean-bound wastewater at the Atlantic City facility [6]. There currently are no state or federal regulations that require the removal of microplastics in wastewater or drinking water [1].

## Impact and future plans

Microplastics can leach into wastewater treatment plants after they're discharged by industrial facilities or collected from stormwater runoff [1]. Residents also contribute to pollution by washing clothes that contain microplastics [1]. The Atlantic County Utilities Authority said it is crucial to remove these contaminants before discharging them into the environment [4]. Wastewater treatment plants discharge their treated effluent into waterways like the Atlantic Ocean [1].

Yidian Liu, PolyGone's co-founder and chief operating officer, noted that the technology stands out for its sleek design influenced by their architecture background [2]. She compared the approach to how complex problems are solved with simple designs in products like the iPhone [2]. The founders say they have launched a similar system for a wastewater treatment plant in California [1]. They are also interested in scaling down the technology for residential uses [1].

In laboratory settings, PolyGone's technology has been able to remove more than 98% of microplastics [7]. There is no data yet for the commercial system, but the founders remain confident it will continue to remove a majority of microplastics [1]. The utility stated that if they do not remove plastic from wastewater, they are putting it back into the environment [1]. These particles have been detected in the human bloodstream and brain tissue, though specific harms are still under research [1].
